It was about three years ago when I had a realization that made me question something I had never really thought about before: how much of who I am, what I think, and the decisions I make are actually mine?

I had started noticing that my thought process was changing. Not necessarily in a way that I could immediately identify as good or bad, but in a way that made me uncomfortable. My opinions were beginning to sound familiar. My arguments were beginning to resemble things I had seen in reels. Even some of the things I considered my own thoughts felt like something I had simply picked up somewhere along the way.

And that bothered me.

I've always been somewhat of a loner when it comes to philosophy, morals, and the way I approach things. Skepticism, perhaps, is a better word to describe it. I've never been particularly comfortable accepting something simply because everyone else seems to agree with it.

Whenever I saw a lot of people doing something, I would wonder, what if doing this is wrong? Whenever I saw people avoiding something, I would wonder, what if avoiding it is wrong? When something was widely considered right, I would still question whether it actually was. And when something was considered terribly wrong, I would sometimes find myself wondering whether there was another side to it that people weren't considering.

It wasn't that I wanted to disagree with everyone. Nor was I trying to defend things that were obviously wrong. If there was evidence right in front of me, I wouldn't dismiss it just to entertain an alternative possibility. But when people's conclusions were based more on opinions, assumptions, or reasoning that didn't seem particularly solid, I always wanted to leave a little room for doubt.

What if we're missing something? What if our reasoning isn't as solid as we think it is? What if there's another way to look at this?

I liked that about myself. I still do.

But somewhere along the way, I felt like I was losing it.

I started noticing that my thoughts were becoming increasingly similar to what I consumed on social media. The same arguments, the same opinions, the same conclusions, sometimes even the same expressions. I would come across a quote from someone, often taken completely out of context, and find myself accepting the idea it presented without really examining it. Not all quotes are wrong, of course. Some are insightful, some are worth remembering, and some can genuinely change the way you look at things. But a quote, especially one presented in isolation to prove a point, doesn't necessarily carry the meaning it originally had.

And I started wondering whether I was actually thinking or simply getting better at repeating things I had seen.

I don't think social media was the only reason. There are always influences around us. News, people, conversations, our surroundings, and even the people we admire shape the way we think. That's probably unavoidable. But social media seemed to have made that process particularly easy. It constantly presented me with opinions, arguments, conclusions, and even instructions on how to live. And the more I consumed them, the harder it became to distinguish between what I had genuinely thought through and what I had simply become familiar with.

There were other things I started noticing, too.

I had developed a strange habit of finding validation for my mistakes on social media. Whenever I did something I knew I shouldn't have done, it wasn't particularly difficult to find someone else who had done the same thing. There are billions of people in the world, after all. Someone, somewhere, has probably made every mistake imaginable.

And somehow, seeing other people make the same mistakes made me feel better about my own.

Instead of regretting what I had done, understanding why it was wrong, and promising myself not to repeat it, I could simply find someone else doing the same thing and convince myself that perhaps it wasn't that bad.

But the fact that other people make the same mistake doesn't make it any less of a mistake, does it?

Then there was comparison.

There is always someone better than you at something. That's not particularly difficult to understand. If you see one or two people doing something better than you, you might make them your inspiration. You learn from them, work harder, and try to improve yourself.

But when you're constantly exposed to hundreds or thousands of people who seem to be doing better than you, it starts feeling different. It becomes difficult to appreciate your own progress when there is always someone several steps ahead of you. Someone younger, more successful, more talented, more knowledgeable, or simply better at something you wish you were good at.

At some point, inspiration starts turning into discouragement. You stop seeing people as examples of what you could achieve and start seeing them as reminders of how far behind you are.

And then there were my friends.

I used to think I had quite a lot of friends. I had people on Facebook, Instagram, and other platforms. There were conversations, interactions, birthday wishes, comments, and all the usual things that make you feel like you're connected to people.

But one day, I decided to actually look at those conversations.

I noticed that most of them had been initiated by me. Most of them were kept alive by me. If I didn't reach out, there was a good chance the conversation would simply stop. Very few people actually initiated conversations with me without needing something or having a particular reason to contact me.

It was a little heartbreaking, but I didn't think too much of it at first.

Then came my birthday.

A lot of people posted birthday wishes on my Facebook wall. Friends, people from my circles, and even family members. There were posts, comments, and public wishes. But when I looked at my phone, very few people had actually messaged or called me personally.

I don't know why, but that bothered me more than I expected.

A public birthday post is nice. I appreciate the gesture, and I don't want to make it sound like people are obligated to call or message me. They're not. But I suppose I had started questioning the difference between being visible to people and actually being remembered by them.

A few days after my birthday, I decided to do something about it.

I decided to leave social media.

Not permanently, at least not initially. I wanted to experiment. I wanted to see what would happen if I simply stopped being available on those platforms. I made a post explaining that I would be using WhatsApp instead of Facebook and Instagram, left it there for about a week, and then deactivated everything.

And then I waited.

A month passed. Then two. Then three. Then four.

There were only a handful of people who actually reached out to me on WhatsApp, apart from my parents. Two or three people, perhaps. And even among them, most conversations happened because someone needed something from me.

That was probably the most heartbreaking part of the entire experiment.

I had spent so much time thinking I had all these friends, only to realize how little of that connection existed outside the platforms that kept us connected. I don't mean that everyone who didn't contact me was pretending to be my friend. People have their own lives, their own responsibilities, and their own ways of maintaining relationships. Some people simply aren't good at initiating conversations.

But I couldn't ignore what I had discovered, either.

Perhaps I had mistaken the existence of conversations for the existence of relationships. Perhaps I had confused being surrounded by people online with actually having people around me.

Or perhaps I had simply expected more from people than I should have.

Whatever the reason, I decided I wasn't going back unless I had a solid reason to.

And it's been almost three years now.

I haven't returned to Facebook or Instagram. I still get influenced by things, obviously. I read news, interact with people, have conversations, and live in the same world as everyone else. I don't think it's possible to exist without being influenced by your surroundings. And I wouldn't necessarily want that, either. Other people can teach us things we would never have discovered on our own.

But I do feel like I'm getting some of my independent thinking back.

I'm questioning things again. I'm becoming more comfortable with not having an immediate opinion about everything. I'm more willing to consider possibilities that aren't particularly popular, and I'm less inclined to accept something simply because I've heard it repeated enough times.

I don't always get it right. I probably never will. But at least I feel like I'm doing more of the thinking myself.

And, honestly, it's been peaceful.

There is something liberating about not constantly knowing what everyone is doing, what everyone thinks, what everyone considers important, or what everyone thinks you should be doing with your life. I don't have to keep up with hundreds of people. I don't have to compare my progress with theirs. I don't have to consume opinions on every possible subject, and I don't have to have an opinion on everything.

But there is a price to it.

I lost almost everyone.

If I leave my phone sitting somewhere for a month or two, and I'm not physically away from my parents or otherwise unreachable, there's a good chance it won't ring. It won't buzz. There won't be messages from people simply wanting to know how I'm doing. Most notifications will be work-related or from someone who needs something.

And sometimes, I wonder whether the gain was worth the sacrifice.

Did I really need to give up so many connections to regain some control over my thoughts? Was leaving social media the right decision, or did I simply exchange one kind of influence for another kind of isolation? Did I become more independent, or did I just become less exposed to perspectives that might have challenged me?

I don't have a definite answer.

I know that I miss having people around. I miss the feeling of being connected, even if some of those connections weren't as meaningful as I once thought. And I won't pretend that being alone all the time is some extraordinary achievement in self-discipline or intellectual independence.

But I also know that I don't particularly miss social media.

It's been almost three years, and I haven't felt the need to go back. Perhaps that says something about how much I needed the break in the first place.

I still wonder, though.

Was the peace worth the loneliness?

Thank you for reading. 🙏
